# Polynesian voyaging: sources and route notes

Research checked September 21, 2026. Story copy is in `tour-stories.md`; the geographic route data is in `tour-polynesia.mjs`.

## Reading the map

The five stages are editorial snapshots: Pleistocene Near Oceania, the Austronesian and Lapita movements into Remote Oceania and Micronesia, the East Polynesian expansion, the far corners of the triangle, and contact with South America. Routes are schematic great-circle arcs between representative islands, not reconstructed canoe tracks, and the moving dots do not count voyages. One-way “settlement” lines mark first crossings whose departure island is inferred; two-way “voyaging” lines mark continuing exchange between islands. The Pacific view moves the two American map pieces to Pacific-facing joins so that these arcs stay continuous across the date line.

## Near Oceania and the Austronesian arrival

- [Te Ara: Pacific migrations](https://teara.govt.nz/en/pacific-migrations). Summarizes settlement of New Guinea, the Bismarck Archipelago and the Solomon Islands tens of thousands of years ago, the long stop at the edge of Near Oceania, and the later Austronesian movement out of island Southeast Asia. The Sahul crossing is shared with the human migrations story (see `human-migrations-sources.md` for the Sahul chronology and its debate) and is drawn fainter here.
- Pleistocene dates for the Bismarcks (about 40,000 years ago), Buka in the Solomons (about 29,000 years ago) and Manus are archaeological consensus figures from cave sites such as Buang Merabak, Matenkupkum, Kilu and Pamwak; the routes between them are inferred. New Britain obsidian reaching New Ireland from about 20,000 years ago is the earliest evidence of interisland exchange in the region and is drawn as a two-way link.
- The Austronesian expansion from Taiwan through the Philippines is a linguistic and archaeological model; the Marianas settlement around 1500 BCE from the Philippines and the later settlement of the Caroline Islands from Melanesia around 2,000 years ago are drawn fainter because departure points and dates remain debated.

## Lapita and West Polynesia

- [Britannica: Lapita culture](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Lapita-culture). Lapita pottery makers spread from the Bismarck Archipelago through island Melanesia to Fiji, Tonga and Samoa in the late second millennium BCE. The drawn order of crossings follows the general west-to-east chronology; individual hops are schematic.
- [Te Ara: Pacific migrations](https://teara.govt.nz/en/pacific-migrations). Places settlement of West Polynesia at about 1100–800 BCE and describes the long pause before East Polynesia was settled after 1000 CE, with New Zealand reached about 1250–1300 CE.

## East Polynesia and the far corners

- [Wilmshurst et al., PNAS (2011): High-precision radiocarbon dating shows recent and rapid initial human colonization of East Polynesia](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1015876108). Reliable dates place central East Polynesian settlement at about 1025–1120 CE and the remote islands, including Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and New Zealand, at about 1190–1290 CE. Departure islands are not given by the dates; Marquesas → Hawaiʻi and Mangareva/Pitcairn → Rapa Nui follow common archaeological and linguistic arguments and are drawn fainter.
- [Collerson & Weisler, Science (2007): Stone adze compositions and the extent of ancient Polynesian voyaging and trade](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1147013). Geochemistry traces a Tuamotu adze to a Hawaiian basalt source, evidence for long two-way voyaging between Hawaiʻi and central East Polynesia. The Hawaiʻi–Society link is drawn fainter because the exact islands and frequency are uncertain.
- [Te Ara: Polynesian languages map](https://teara.govt.nz/en/map/43839/polynesian-languages). Defines the cultural region used for the triangle. The Kermadec and Chatham crossings are drawn fainter: they are known from archaeology and Moriori tradition rather than dated voyages, and Chatham settlement is generally placed around 1500 CE.

## Contact with South America

- [Ioannidis et al., Nature (2020): Native American gene flow into Polynesia predating Easter Island settlement](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-020-2487-2). Finds Native American ancestry in eastern Polynesian populations, closest to Indigenous peoples of present-day Colombia and Ecuador, with admixture dated to around 1200 CE. The authors do not resolve where the meeting occurred; the Marquesas–coast line is one hypothesis and is drawn with sparse dots and an uncertain style.
- [Moreno-Mayar et al., Nature (2024): Ancient Rapanui genomes reveal resilience and pre-European contact with the Americas](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07881-4). Ancient Rapanui genomes carry Native American ancestry with admixture estimated around 1250–1430 CE, before European arrival in 1722. This supports contact but does not determine its direction.
- [Roullier et al., PNAS (2013): Historical collections reveal patterns of diffusion of sweet potato in Oceania obscured by modern plant movements and recombination](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1211049110). Supports a pre-European introduction of the South American sweet potato into Polynesia. The plant does not itself show who carried it.

## Deliberate limits

Micronesian and later Austronesian movements, Fijian and Melanesian exchange networks, and the end of long-distance voyaging in the 15th century are mentioned only in passing. The coordinates are representative islands; short arcs between them do not indicate actual sailing routes, seasonal winds or navigation methods. The contact lines remain hypotheses with uncertain direction and should not be read as a Polynesian settlement of South America or the reverse.
